meta.regime: The war premium came back within twenty-four hours of being sold. Thursday's news that the Trump administration told mediators it has no interest in returning to the June deal terms sent crude up roughly 3% from Wednesday's low and pushed European gas back to a January-2023 high on its third consecutive weekly gain, which re-arms the inflation impulse in every energy-importing currency and rescues the two currencies that were marked down yesterday for owning it. The regime is therefore not de-escalation and not escalation but a violently two-way headline market layered on top of an unresolved policy question, and the single most informative fact of the session is what did NOT happen: neither gold nor the Swiss franc bid on the re-escalation. Both fell. The haven complex has stopped trading the Strait and started trading the Fed, which is why Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote at 14:00Z is the largest single item on the board.
meta.nextBigEvent: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote, today at 14:00Z (10:00 ET) - a chair with no policy record, speaking into a market pricing roughly a one-in-three September hike, with energy re-inflating and the labour market still the weak leg. Spain's flash CPI at 07:00Z and Canadian Q2 GDP at 12:30Z land first.

dailyRead: Yesterday this board argued that the de-escalation trade had moved past its first victim and was claiming its second and third, and it explicitly warned that the whole thing was one headline away from reversing. That headline arrived the same afternoon. The Trump administration told mediators it has no interest in returning to the terms of the preliminary deal reached with Iran in June, and the energy complex re-priced immediately: WTI is 82.96 against 80.57 yesterday, Brent 88.07 against 86.49, and European TTF gas is 68.73 EUR/MWh and back toward its highest level since January 2023, up more than 3% on the week for a third straight weekly gain, with EU storage still only about 63% full and Qatari LNG still disrupted by the near-closure of the Strait. Two of yesterday's three score changes therefore have to be reversed, and one is confirmed. New Zealand goes back to plus 1, and the correction is more than an oil call. A Reuters poll published overnight has 27 of 31 economists - 90% - expecting a 25bp hike to 2.75% on September 2, with two-thirds looking for at least one more this year and a median year-end OCR of 3.0%, and economists explicitly do not expect inflation back inside the 1-3% band this year partly because of energy. That is not the three-way coin flip described yesterday, and with petrol prices re-inflating the transport component that drove the 4.1% Q2 print, the hawkish case is re-armed rather than disarmed. What still caps the kiwi at plus 1 rather than higher is genuinely weak domestic data: unemployment 5.6% and the highest since Q3 2015, underutilisation 13.8%, wage growth 2.1%, consumer confidence collapsing to 80.4 from 94.7 and the manufacturing PMI down to 54.3 from 60.1. NZD/USD is 0.59579. Canada is upgraded from minus 1 to zero. The loonie's engine is running again, and the growth data is about to be much better than the score implied: RBC has raised its Q2 estimate to plus 3.4% annualised from 1.7% on the monthly readings, with exports seen up 18.3% annualised against imports up 6.3%, adding 3.3 points to GDP. The reason this is an upgrade to zero and not to plus 1 is that the composition is almost entirely a net-export rebound after a negative Q1 - the Bank of Canada's own July minutes doubted the sustainability of exactly this bounce given the tariff escalation - and the C$27.6bn retaliation on roughly 700 US product lines at 15, 25 and 50 per cent still starts on September 8 against domestic services at 49.1 and retail sales at minus 0.8%. Q2 GDP lands today at 12:30Z and decides whether zero holds. Switzerland stays at zero and this is now the highest-confidence call on the board, because it was tested and passed. On a day the war premium came back, the franc did not bid: USD/CHF rose to 0.80512, EUR/CHF is still pinned near 0.938, and gold fell below 4,600 from a three-month high. The franc's haven leg is not weak, it is absent, and what is left is 0.4% CPI at a four-month low, 0.3% core, deflating producer and import prices, unemployment up to 3.0%, an SNB anchored at zero through 2027 and openly readier to intervene. The euro holds plus 2 and its case got harder rather than softer. Yesterday's July accounts said the pause should not be read as the end of the tightening cycle and that another hike is likely unless the inflation outlook improves significantly, with some members saying they would not have opposed a July move; Reuters reports that governors are now ready to raise the deposit rate to 2.50% on September 10. Read the caveat honestly - the accounts also stressed avoiding pre-commitment and wanted the September decision kept open - but the direction is one-way, and the gas move strengthens the inflation argument the ECB has been citing. Spain's flash August CPI at 07:00Z is the immediate catalyst, coming off a July print revised UP to 3.6% with the harmonised rate at 3.9%, a two-and-a-half-year high driven by diesel at 15.7% and petrol at 7.3% - precisely the channel that just re-opened. Japan holds plus 1 with the best data of the session: Tokyo core CPI printed 1.8% against 1.7% expected, a five-month high and a third straight monthly acceleration, core-core held at exactly 2.0%, and the national jobless rate fell to 2.4%, the lowest in a year, while Himino publicly stressed the need for timely rate hikes. That removes the soft-consensus risk that pushed USD/JPY to MEDIUM yesterday. The pair is 159.475 and pressing 160, which since the August 1 joint US-Japan intervention has functioned as a political line in the sand - the MoF playbook of jawboning, rate-checking and then acting sits directly on the same side as the trade, which is why USD/JPY goes back to a HIGH-conviction short. The offset is that re-inflating crude reopens Japan's import-price problem, so this is a policy trade, not a terms-of-trade trade. Australia holds plus 1 on a trimmed mean stuck at 3.6%, the G10's highest cash rate at 4.35%, September 29 hike odds around 27% and copper at 6.5962 just under its record, against a labour market that shed 15,827 jobs in July with unemployment at a post-COVID 4.5%. Sterling holds plus 1 on the highest yield in the G10 near 5.0% with cable at 1.35901, and note that UK gas at 169.27 GBp/therm and up 14.19% on the month re-opens the Ofgem channel that the three BoE dissenters need. The dollar stays at minus 1: nothing in the TE data changed - CPI 3.4%, core 2.5%, unemployment 4.1%, payrolls minus 23,000 - and everything now hangs on Warsh at 14:00Z, into roughly one-in-three odds of a September hike and an energy shock that argues for tightening at the same time as a labour market that argues against it. The practical book: take the yen trade with size, take the euro against the dollar and the franc, and cut size on the loonie shorts because their premise just changed. And keep the symmetry in mind - this trade reversed in a day once and can reverse again, so the geopolitical legs (USOIL, XAU, GER40) carry deliberately smaller conviction than the policy legs.

USD.when: Sept 15-16 FOMC - hold remains the base case, with September hike odds around one-in-three and the year-end path unresolved
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning and NOTHING moved: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% from 3.5%, core 2.5%, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000, GDP growth 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%. The July 29 decision was a 9-3 hold with all three dissents FOR a hike, and four regional Reserve Banks separately sought a discount-rate increase. Wednesday's data gave the dollar its reprieve - core PCE +0.2% m/m and 3.3% y/y in line rather than the feared 0.3%, headline PCE 3.7%, Q2 GDP confirmed UNREVISED with personal consumption +3.4%, claims 206k - and Collins said on Aug 25 that tightening soon will be appropriate absent sustained progress. Today's re-inflation of crude and European gas pushes in the same hawkish direction. Against all of that sits the labour market, which is the only genuinely weak leg and the reason the score is minus 1 rather than zero. Everything now routes through one event: Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote at 14:00Z, 10:00 ET, on a symposium theme of financial innovation and payments. He has no policy record as Chair, market estimates of September hike odds range widely from roughly a quarter to two-thirds depending on the source, and Treasury yields are near 4.7%. Keep dollar-leg size reduced until it is delivered, and note that the cleanest dollar expression today is against the yen rather than a broad short - DXY is only a LOW-conviction ticket into this.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z - TE model carries 2.65% refi (2.50% depo); Reuters reports governors ready to move
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike; main refinancing 2.40%. Use 2.25%. EUR holds +2 and yesterday's accounts made the case harder to argue against. The July minutes state that all policymakers agreed to hold but that some would not have opposed another hike, that the likelihood of further tightening becoming unnecessary remained low, and - twice - that the pause should NOT be interpreted as the end of the tightening cycle, with another hike likely unless the inflation outlook improves significantly. Reuters sources say those doubts have since cleared and governors are ready to raise to 2.50% on September 9-10. The honest caveat, straight from the same accounts: policymakers stressed clear communication to avoid pre-commitment and wanted the September decision kept open. TE macro re-verified unchanged: HICP 2.9% with core 2.5% and services 3.4%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, unemployment 6.3%, manufacturing PMI 52.8 at a four-year high, services 51.7. The energy argument that had weakened yesterday is fully restored - TTF is 68.73 EUR/MWh, back toward its highest since January 2023, up more than 3% on the week for a third straight weekly gain, with storage near 63% and Qatari LNG still disrupted. Immediate catalyst: Spain's flash August CPI at 07:00Z, off a July print revised UP to 3.6% with the harmonised rate at 3.9%, a February-2023 high, on diesel 15.7% and petrol 7.3% - the exact transmission channel that just reopened. Counterweights unchanged: negotiated wages 2.44% from 2.56%, consumer inflation expectations down a third month to 2.9%, and a gas shock that is a terms-of-trade hit as well as an inflation impulse.

GBP.when: Sept 17, 11:00Z - Jul 30 was a 6-3 hold with three voting for 4.00%
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%. GBP holds +1 and still trades on yield rather than policy: the 10-year gilt near 4.99% remains the highest in the G10, with cable at 1.35901 after a six-month high of 1.3670 on Aug 21. TE macro re-verified: CPI 2.9% from 2.6%, GDP +0.4% q/q and 1.2% y/y, unemployment 4.9%, employment change +83k, services PMI 52.8 and manufacturing 51.5. The underlying inflation picture is genuinely two-sided - July's rise was the 13% Ofgem cap uplift with energy inflation at 9.8%, while core held FLAT at 2.6% for a third month and services COOLED to 3.4% - which is why this is +1 on carry rather than +1 on policy. What changed today is that the escalation path for the three dissenters reopened: UK gas is 169.27 GBp/therm and up 14.19% on the month, so the administered-energy channel that produced the July print is re-inflating into the next cap window. There is no UK data of consequence before September 17. Express sterling against the loonie, the dollar and the franc; do not express it against the euro, the Aussie, the kiwi or the yen, where the gaps are one notch or zero.

JPY.when: Sept 18, 03:00Z - roughly 80% priced for +25bp to 1.25%, and the overnight data reinforced it
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, the highest since September 1995, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%; the board warned underlying inflation could exceed 2%. JPY holds +1 and got the cleanest data of the session. Tokyo August core CPI printed 1.8% against 1.7% expected, a five-month high and a third consecutive monthly acceleration, with core-core holding exactly at the 2% target and headline at 1.9%; Tokyo leads the national print by about three weeks. The national jobless rate fell to 2.4% from 2.5%, the lowest in a year. Deputy Governor Himino publicly stressed the need for timely rate hikes. That is a clean sweep against yesterday's soft consensus, and it is why USD/JPY goes back from MEDIUM to a HIGH-conviction short. National CPI 1.9% and a seven-month high, core 1.8%, services PPI +3.6% y/y, cash earnings +3.4% with real earnings positive a sixth month, manufacturing PMI 55.1 at a four-month high. The tape is the argument for the trade rather than against it: USD/JPY is 159.475 and pressing 160, which since the first joint US-Japan intervention since 2011 on Aug 1 - after a 40-year high of 163.73 drove the pair to 155-156 - has functioned as a political line in the sand. Both Tokyo and Washington say they stand ready to act again, and the standard MoF sequence into that level is jawboning, then rate-checking, then intervention. The honest offset is that re-inflating crude reopens the import-price drag, +29.1% y/y, that has capped the yen all year, so treat this as a policy trade, not a terms-of-trade trade. The BoJ's quarterly outlook cut FY2026 inflation to 2.5% and lifted FY2026 growth to 0.6%.

AUD.when: Sept 29, 04:30Z - hike odds around 27% after the July CPI beat
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, the G10's highest, held Aug 11. AUD holds +1 on the same two legs as yesterday, both intact. The monetary leg is the July CPI indicator: headline +1.0% m/m against 0.8% forecast with the annual rate 3.5% from 3.8%, and critically the RBA's preferred trimmed mean +0.5% m/m against 0.3%, leaving the annual trimmed mean UNCHANGED at 3.6%, its highest since September 2024. The breadth is what matters - market goods and services excluding volatile items +1.0% m/m and discretionary ex tobacco +1.5% - which is demand-side rather than a petrol blip, and unlike New Zealand's print it does not depend on which way the Strait of Hormuz goes. It validates the August minutes, where the Board weighed a pre-emptive hike, called inflation too high with excess demand persisting, did not discuss a cut, and named Middle East oil and AI capex as upside risks; Hauser said on Aug 19 the Bank will need to raise again if those risks materialise. The industrial leg is copper at 6.5962 USD/lb, just under its record, on LME stocks halved since mid-May, the Kamoa-Kakula flood and heavy US tariff front-running. What keeps this at +1 and not +2 is the labour market: July employment FELL 15,827 with part-time down 32,160, unemployment 4.5% at a post-COVID high, wage growth 3.2%. TE re-verified GDP annual growth 2.5% with the quarterly rate 0.3%; Q2 GDP lands Sept 2 at 01:30Z with a TE forecast of 0.0% q/q, which is the soft counterweight to the CPI beat.

NZD.when: Sept 2, 02:00Z - UPGRADED back to a hike: a Reuters poll has 27 of 31 economists (90%) expecting +25bp to 2.75%
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.50% after the Jul 8 hike, the first in three years, taken on a 3-3 committee split with Governor Breman casting the deciding vote. NZD is RESTORED from 0 to +1 and the correction has two independent parts. First, the pricing: a Reuters poll published overnight has 27 of 31 economists - 90% - expecting a 25bp hike to 2.75% on September 2, two-thirds expecting at least one further hike this quarter, and a median year-end OCR of 3.0%, with the September decision expected to be reached by consensus rather than a casting vote. That is not the three-way event yesterday's file described, and the correction stands on its own regardless of oil. Second, the premise of yesterday's downgrade has been reversed: the argument was that the 4.1% Q2 CPI was a petrol print - transport +10.6%, petrol +27.5% - and that with the RBNZ's own July MPS naming the partial reopening of Hormuz as the reason headline falls back toward 2%, falling crude would disarm it. Crude is not falling; it is 82.96 and up roughly 3% from Wednesday's low, and economists explicitly do not expect inflation back inside the 1-3% band this year partly because of energy. What still caps the kiwi at +1 rather than higher is a genuinely soft domestic economy: unemployment 5.6% and the highest since Q3 2015, underutilisation 13.8% from 12.9%, wage growth 2.1%, two-year inflation expectations 2.34%, consumer confidence down to 80.4 from 94.7, manufacturing PMI 54.3 from 60.1, and TE's Q3 GDP forecast at MINUS 0.1% q/q for September 16. NZD/USD 0.59579. Trade the kiwi long against the dollar, the loonie and the franc; keep it flat against the yen, the Aussie and sterling, where the gap is zero.

CAD.when: Sept 2, 13:45Z - a seventh straight hold (note: sources conflict between Sept 2 and Sept 3)
CAD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 2.25%, held Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting; Bank Rate 2.5%, deposit 2.20%. CAD is UPGRADED from -1 to 0. Two things changed. The oil engine restarted - WTI 82.96 and Brent 88.07 after the Trump administration told mediators it has no interest in the June deal terms - and the growth data is about to look far better than the score implied: RBC has lifted its Q2 GDP estimate to +3.4% annualised from 1.7% on the monthly readings, with exports seen +18.3% annualised against imports +6.3%, adding 3.3 points. TE also re-verified an improved manufacturing PMI at 53.5 from 53.0 and business confidence at 55.1. Be precise about why this is an upgrade to ZERO and not to +1. The GDP bounce is almost entirely a net-export rebound after a negative Q1, and the Bank's own July 15 minutes recorded doubts about the sustainability of exactly that bounce given the tariff escalation; the domestic economy underneath is still soft with services at 49.1, retail sales -0.8% m/m and annual GDP growth at -0.1%. And the trade war is unchanged: Champagne's 99-page list covers C$27.6bn, about US$19.9bn, across roughly 700 American product lines at 15%, 25% and 50% from September 8, matching new US 50% duties on about US$20bn of Canadian imports, with a C$7.5bn domestic support package alongside. CPI is 3.0% at the ceiling of the control range with gasoline +25.7% y/y, and re-inflating crude pushes that higher. Q2 GDP today at 12:30Z, consensus +3.4% annualised against -0.1% prior with June monthly at +0.2%, decides whether zero holds or the score has to move again. USD/CAD 1.38511. Cut size on every loonie short - the premise changed overnight.

CHF.when: Sept 24, 07:30Z - Reuters poll unanimously expects zero, held through 2026
CHF.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 0.00%, held Mar 19 and Jun 18. CHF stays at 0, and unlike the other two downgrades from yesterday this one was tested overnight and PASSED, which makes it the highest-confidence call on the board. The test was simple: the war premium came back - crude up roughly 3%, European gas back toward a January-2023 high - and the franc did not bid. USD/CHF ROSE to 0.80512, up 0.11% on the day and 0.46% on the week, EUR/CHF remains pinned near 0.938 against the strongest currency on the board, and gold fell below 4,600 from a three-month high on the very same news. The haven leg is not weak, it is absent, and the whole complex has switched to trading the Fed instead of the Strait. What remains is a funding-currency profile, re-verified on TE: July CPI 0.4% from 0.5% and a four-month low with the first monthly fall in six, core 0.3%, producer and import prices deflating, unemployment risen to 3.0% with 139,276 unemployed, wage growth 1.8%, and an SNB forecast of just 0.6% inflation for 2026 and 2027. The central bank is on the other side of any franc strength: Schlegel has repeated his readiness to intervene against rapid or excessive appreciation and FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July. geopolitics: The single most important fact of the session is that the de-escalation trade lasted one day. Yesterday's board argued the unwind was claiming its second and third currency victims and warned explicitly that the whole structure was one headline away from reversing; that headline arrived the same afternoon, when the Trump administration told mediators it has no interest in returning to the terms of the preliminary deal reached with Iran in June. The energy complex re-priced immediately. WTI is 82.96 against 80.57 yesterday, Brent 88.07 against 86.49, European TTF gas is 68.73 EUR/MWh and back toward its highest since January 2023 after a third straight weekly gain of more than 3%, German gas rose 3.79% to 68.79, UK gas is up 14.19% on the month and coal jumped 6.29%. The underlying political picture is a stack of partial agreements none of which actually opens the waterway. Iran and Oman announced a phased framework on Aug 25 - a temporary joint navigation corridor with the inbound leg in Iranian waters and the outbound leg through Iranian and Omani waters, joint mine-clearing, and 30-to-60-day technical talks - and have since added a revenue-sharing agreement over the Strait, but Tehran stresses that this does not guarantee an immediate reopening. The IRGC said on Aug 26 that the United States is the obstacle and the Strait stays CLOSED until Washington honours the Islamabad memorandum, with a senior official demanding an end to the war plus financial compensation, and Araghchi has said Iran will accept an end to the war but not a ceasefire. Against that sits Bessent's Aug 23-24 sanctions package on aviation, shipping, technology, gold and digital assets, Trump's Aug 17 refusal to extend the ceasefire, and Qatari mediation in Tehran this week. The one genuine counterweight to the bullish energy read is physical rather than political: Goldman Sachs estimates Persian Gulf crude exports have recovered to 15-16 million barrels a day, roughly two-thirds of pre-war levels and well above the 5-6 million barrel trough in March, helped by US bombing that degraded Iranian radar and maritime surveillance and by tankers running dark at night. The flows are healing even as the framework stalls, which is why USOIL is a LOW-MED long rather than a conviction one. The FX transmission today runs backwards through yesterday's file. NZD returns to +1 because its petrol-driven CPI is re-arming and, independently, because 90% of economists now expect a Sept 2 hike. CAD returns to 0 because its oil engine restarted, capped there only by the Sept 8 tariff wall. EUR is reinforced at +2 because the gas leg the ECB keeps citing came straight back. And the most telling FX fact of all is a negative one: neither gold nor the Swiss franc bid on this. Gold fell below 4,600 from a three-month high and USD/CHF rose to 0.80512. The haven complex has stopped pricing the Strait and started pricing the Fed, which is why the CHF downgrade is now the highest-confidence call on this board and why Warsh at 14:00Z outranks every geopolitical headline on the calendar today.
